title: How Death Masks Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore death masks: their history from ancient Egypt and Mycenaean gold masks through Roman ancestor masks, Italian and European practice, Madame Tussaud and Philippe Curtius after the French Revolution, and the 19th-century phrenology craze. They cover notable death masks (John Dillinger, Sir Walter Scott, Abraham Lincoln's life mask, Edwin Booth, John Merrick, Napoleon, George Bernard Shaw, Nikola Tesla), the Lawrence Hutton collection at Princeton, the process of making a death mask, the Unknown Woman of the Seine mask that inspired Resusci Annie for CPR training, and the Scotland Yard Crime Museum. The episode closes with a TV show announcement and a listener mail correction about peak oil and fracking.
topics: making a death mask plaster bandages

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with casual banter about plaster craft, a movie dance scene parody, and their departments having a party without them.

segments.title: John Dillinger's death and death mask
segments.summary: John Dillinger is killed by FBI agents outside a Chicago movie theater after being betrayed. Authorized casts of his face were made after death, and J. Edgar Hoover reportedly kept a positive in his office. The hosts compare it to public displays of outlaws like Jesse James.

segments.title: Ancient origins: Egyptians and Mycenaeans
segments.summary: Death masks trace back at least to Egypt, where funerary masks helped the soul find the body and face in the afterlife. Mycenaeans made rough gold funerary masks, and less wealthy people could have linen or papyrus masks.

segments.title: Roman ancestor masks and early European practice
segments.summary: Romans wore death masks of deceased relatives at funerals. Julius Caesar had a full wax cast of his body made, which Mark Antony displayed, provoking a riot. Artists used death masks as references, and in Europe outside Italy the practice was mostly limited to nobles and the wealthy until late modern times.

segments.title: Madame Tussaud and French Revolution death masks
segments.summary: Madame Tussaud and her uncle Philippe Curtius made death masks during the French Revolution, including of a mistress of Louis XVI who was guillotined. Curtius reshaped the decapitated face and the Tussaud wax museum grew out of this work.

segments.title: Death masks in the Victorian era and phrenology
segments.summary: Death masks were displayed as status symbols in homes. Phrenology, the idea that personality and criminality could be read from skull shape, increased demand for death masks, including of John Merrick, for side-by-side comparison. The hosts say the theory was wrong.

segments.title: Medical clues from death masks and famous examples
segments.summary: Death masks can hint at cause of death: Sir Walter Scott's mask suggests a stroke, and Lincoln's life masks may suggest a wasting disease. Edwin Booth's mask was collected by Lawrence Hutton, a Harper's editor who built the largest collection of death masks and bequeathed it to Princeton.

segments.title: Princeton's Lawrence Hutton death mask museum and detail
segments.summary: The hosts describe the digitized Lawrence Hutton Death Mask Museum website and the eerie detail of masks, such as the Dillinger mask showing abrasions and the bullet hole. They mention a Princeton brewpub.

segments.title: How a death mask is made
segments.summary: The mask must be made soon after death before bloating sets in. Grease is applied to the face, especially facial hair, and plaster bandages are laid on in layers, with the first layer capturing the detail. Plaster once took about an hour to set and now takes minutes. The negative mold can then be cast in wax, bronze, or marble, as with Napoleon's mask.

segments.title: Unknown Woman of the Seine and Resusci Anne
segments.summary: The Unknown Woman of the Seine mask, popular in 19th-century Paris, is said to be from a drowned woman, but the hosts note the story is doubtful and the mask may be from a live model. The mask was later used by Asmund Laerdal and Peter Safar for Resusci Anne, the CPR training dummy.

segments.title: Scotland Yard Black Museum and closing mentions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Scotland Yard's Black Museum, now called the Crime Museum, which holds death masks, nooses, weapons, and reportedly letters from Jack the Ripper.

segments.title: Show business and listener mail
segments.summary: Chuck announces a Science Channel TV show premiering January 19 and the hosts read listener mail from Martha correcting points about peak oil (fossil fuel source material, proved reserves audits) and fracking.
